summary: Specifies the HTTP-based protocol for SCIM, a standardized service for managing identities across multiple domains, such as between an enterprise and cloud providers. It defines how to create, read, search, update and delete identity resources.

plainLanguage.summary: SCIM defines HTTP requests that let one system manage identity records held by another. It uses JSON for users, groups, searches, updates, and error responses.

questions: how does scim use http to manage users
what is a scim bulk request
subtitle: HTTP operations for creating, finding, changing, and deleting identity resources.

tldr.problem: Organizations need a consistent way to manage identity resources across service providers instead of writing a separate integration for each provider.
tldr.mechanism: SCIM maps resource operations to HTTP methods and JSON messages. It defines resource endpoints, search filters, PUT and PATCH updates, bulk requests, and feature-discovery endpoints.
tldr.outcome: Clients can manage users and groups through a standard HTTP interface. RFC 7644 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967.

today: RFC 7644 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2015. It has been updated by RFC 9865 and RFC 9967, and has not been obsoleted. The companion schema is defined in RFC 7643.

sections.title: The SCIM Protocol
sections.content:
The System for Cross-domain Identity Management (SCIM) protocol manages identity data across organizations and services. It uses HTTP requests and JSON bodies with the media type application/scim+json. The resource definitions and attributes are specified in RFC 7643.

SCIM is designed for environments where providers may support different subsets of the schema. The server interprets each request using its own schema and returns the state it actually stored, which may differ from the client's input.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM uses web requests to manage identity records held by a service. The server applies its own schema rules and reports what it saved.

sections.title: Authentication and Authorization
sections.content:
SCIM does not define its own authentication system. It relies on TLS and standard HTTP authentication methods, such as client certificates, bearer tokens, cookies, or other supported schemes. A provider must advertise its supported schemes using WWW-Authenticate and map each authenticated client to an access policy.

The service provider decides which resources each client may read or change. HTTP Basic authentication is discouraged as a single factor because it depends on a relatively static secret. A deployment may permit limited anonymous requests, such as registration, but needs safeguards.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM uses the web's existing ways to verify clients. The provider must also decide which resources each client may access.

sections.title: Endpoints and Basic Operations
sections.content:
The standard endpoints include /Users and /Groups. GET retrieves resources, POST creates them, PUT replaces attributes, PATCH changes part of a resource, and DELETE removes a resource. PUT must not create a new resource. The /Me path can refer to the resource associated with the authenticated subject.

Clients can discover resource endpoints through /ResourceTypes, provider capabilities through /ServiceProviderConfig, and schemas through /Schemas. A successful create returns 201 Created and the new resource's location; a successful delete returns 204 No Content.
sections.plainLanguage: SCIM uses familiar HTTP methods to work with users and groups. Discovery endpoints tell a client which resource types, schemas, and optional features a provider offers.

sections.title: Searching, Filtering, and Paging
sections.content:
Clients can query one resource, an endpoint such as /Users, or the service root. Search responses include a result count and may include a page of resources. Filtering is optional for providers; supported filters can compare values, test whether an attribute is present, combine conditions, or group tests on multi-valued fields.

Sorting and paging can further limit results. The startIndex parameter is one-based and defaults to 1. Paging is not stateful, so clients must allow for results to change between requests. A POST to a .search endpoint can carry filters in the body instead of the URI.
sections.plainLanguage: A search can select matching resources, sort them, and return one page at a time. A POST search puts the filter in the request body instead of the web address.

sections.title: Replacing, Patching, and Deleting
sections.content:
PUT replaces a resource's attributes, subject to each attribute's mutability rules. A server ignores read-only attributes. PATCH applies a sequence of add, remove, or replace operations to selected paths. A PATCH request is atomic: if an operation fails, the server restores the original resource. PATCH is optional, though providers should support it.

DELETE removes a resource from future operations and searches. A provider may retain its data internally, but later requests must treat the resource as not found. Successful deletion returns 204 No Content.
sections.plainLanguage: PUT replaces a resource, while PATCH changes selected fields. A PATCH either completes all its operations or leaves the resource unchanged.

sections.title: Bulk Operations
sections.content:
Bulk is an optional feature that sends several POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE operations in one request to /Bulk. The response reports a status and location for each operation. A client can assign each new resource a temporary bulkId and use that name to refer to it in another operation before the server assigns its permanent id.

The provider normally continues after individual failures. A client may set failOnErrors to stop after a chosen number of failures. Providers can reorder operations only if the final result preserves the client's intent, and must try to resolve circular references.
sections.plainLanguage: Bulk sends several changes in one request. Temporary names let one operation refer to a resource that another operation is creating.

sections.title: Errors and Status Codes
sections.content:
SCIM uses HTTP status codes and also returns a JSON error body with the status, an optional SCIM-specific error type, and optional human-readable detail. For example, a 409 Conflict can report a duplicate resource; a 412 Precondition Failed can mean the resource changed; and 413 Payload Too Large can reject an oversized bulk request.

For bad requests, SCIM error types distinguish cases such as invalidFilter, uniqueness, mutability, invalidSyntax, noTarget, and sensitive information in a URI. These details help a client understand why the server rejected an operation.
sections.plainLanguage: An error response gives both an HTTP status and a SCIM-specific reason. A client can use that reason to tell a bad filter from a duplicate name or a change that is not allowed.

sections.title: Protecting Identity Data
sections.content:
SCIM resources contain sensitive personal information and may contain passwords. Clients and providers must use transport security; providers must support TLS 1.2, and clients must check the server's identity. Bearer tokens and cookies must be unpredictable and sent over TLS; tokens must also have a limited lifetime.

Filters in GET request URIs may expose personal data in browser history or server logs. The RFC recommends POST search for sensitive filters. Providers that allow anonymous creation should limit requests and use safeguards such as secondary confirmation.
sections.plainLanguage: Identity data must travel over a secure connection. Put sensitive search terms in a POST body, not a web address that may be logged.
